March 2, 2022 EPA PFAS Webinar with Public Comment

My name is Carolyn Mahlum-Jenkins and I live in La Crosse, Wisconsin. The Town of Campbell is a bedroom community of La Crosse and there are 4,319 residents. In the winter of 2020/spring of 2021, 555 wells were tested for PFAS and out of those 97% indicated levels of PFAS. The level of PFAS varied between 2 ppt. to over 2000 ppt. The residents have been drinking the contaminated water for 6 years without being notified. Two city of La Crosse wells and private wells are impacted. The Wisconsin Department of Natural Resources and Department of Health Services issued a health advisory at that time.

On Feb. 23, 2022, the State of Wisconsin Natural Resources Board meet to discuss the proposed WDNR standard of 20 ppt. for two of the most studied PFAS compounds-PFOA and PFOS. The Natural Resources Board amended the proposed Drinking Water rule, changing the maximum contaminate level (MCL) for PFOA and PFOS combined to 70 ppt. to match the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency’s Health Advisory level for the same compounds. This was an upward adjustment from the 20 ppt. standard initially proposed by WDNR and most Wisconsinites that have knowledge of the PFAS felt that 20 ppt. combined was too high. The ruling made on Feb. 23, 2022 by the Wisconsin Natural Resources Board has demonstrated that they have turned their backs on Wisconsinites.

Over the past year the number of PFAS contamination sites that the WDNR has taken regulatory action over has grown to more than 50+ sites in 25 communities. The toxic PFAS chemicals have affected residents in communities both large and small contaminating public and private wells. These residents can’t drink, cook, bathe, and water their gardens daily with their water source. Not only do these residents have to put up with the inconvenience of not being able to “turn on their tap” and get safe drinking water, they unfortunately have to live with the anxiety and fear of what the PFAS is doing in their bodies to their organs.

It is known that PFAS accumulates in the blood, tissue and organs. Reputable people and organizations have done some very solid science. We know that there is a direct correlation between elevated PFAS levels in breast milk and elevated levels of PFAS in those infants. We know that PFAS accumulates in the body causing multiple cancers, autoimmune diseases, and resistance to vaccine effectiveness. The federal agency for Toxic Substances and Disease Studies (ATSDR) reports PFAS has been detected in human tissue and organs decades after initial exposure, despite no further ingestion. Again the “forever chemical” is raising havoc in water, air and sediments. Plant life, animals, and humans are being adversely impacted as well. Their property values have plummeted. Residents in the Town of Campbell lives have changed and they are just one community, what about the other 24 communities facing the same predicament in Wisconsin.

What can the EPA do? Take immediate action.
•All unnecessary PFAS should be eliminated/not produced
•Establish a safe PFAS drinking water standard nationally
•Establish safe surface & groundwater standards nationally
(Water does not know borders or boundaries-inter state)
•Establish safe drinking water standard so the FDA starts to protect consumers from bottled water and other water based bottled beverages
•Provide federal recourse for states that do not comply with enforcing established regulations
•Involve PFAS exposed individuals in biomonitoring studies that can provide physicians and public health officials with reference values so that they can determine whether or not people have been exposed to higher levels of PFAS than are found in the general population. Biomonitoring data can also help scientists plan and conduct research on exposure and adverse health effects. Utilize the national biomonitoring data to learn about best practices and outcomes
•Develop a PFAS national biomonitoring data base (for those willing to participate) to track health indicators and impacts on health
•PFAS should be regulated and managed as a single chemical class
•PFAS should be categorized as a “hazardous substance” for clean-up funding
